A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ByteSampler work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original inference-cost measurements, English and Chinese prediction experiments, and downstream ensemble and proxy-tuning results.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds runtime benchmarks, invalid-token analyses, tokenizer validation, and code-completion experiments.

M1.justification: The core covering-tree, pairwise-pruning, and streaming procedures remain. Appendix F adds token-level sampling transformations before aggregation into byte probabilities; v1 Appendix E only discussed the mismatch between byte-level and token-level transformations. Other expanded tokenizer-handling passages primarily provide implementation documentation.

E1.justification: v3 adds substantive code-completion evaluation using HumanEval Random Span with the suffix discarded, extending beyond v1's illustrative code examples. It also reports tokenizer-correctness testing on at least 1 GB of Pile fragments. The original English, Chinese, ensemble, and proxy-tuning task coverage remains.

E2.justification: v3 newly evaluates Beam Summing at beam sizes 1, 3, 10, and 128 in Tables 10–11; v1 mentions beam search but reports no such comparison. Existing comparator families largely remain. The corresponding Phan-method rows retain identical numerical results despite updated naming and attribution.

E3.justification: The original evaluation protocols largely remain, but Appendices E–F introduce substantial new designs: controlled latency workloads, shared-vLLM beam comparisons with losses restricted to jointly successful examples, prefix-only code evaluation using pass@1, and matched byte/token decoding settings. The new Phan timing comparison explicitly uses different 7B models, so it is not a same-model speed comparison.

E4.justification: v3 adds invalid-next-token masking analyses for OLMo2 1B and 7B, beam-width sensitivity and empty-beam failure analysis, tokenizer-correctness checks, and controlled comparisons of decoding transformations at byte versus token level. These examine assumptions, robustness, and decoding behavior that v1 did not experimentally investigate.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without uncertainty intervals. v3 adds 95% confidence intervals to proxy-tuning results, bounds the ensemble confidence intervals, reports uncertainty summaries for new measurements, and specifies 30 runs per method for the standard-sampling timing comparison. This does not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: Tables 9–15 add runtime, beam-failure, masking, code-completion, and decoding results, including ByteSampler versus naive pass@1 of 0.824 versus 0.565. Original ensemble, proxy-tuning, and character-accuracy point estimates remain unchanged. Normalized losses are corrected: for example, ByteSampler's English bits per character changes from 0.81 to 0.87 and Chinese from 3.23 to 3.43, with unchanged raw losses.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds compactness, pairwise-validity, and prefix-probability proofs beyond v1's informal arguments. It revises whole-sequence-validity conditioning to prompt-covering validity and explains local canonicalization under repeated sampling. Table 1 also changes Back Tokenization's CPU complexity from exponential to linear, although v3's prose still describes exponential overhead.

C1.justification: The central claims about PBP correction, byte-level conversion, ensembling, and proxy-tuning remain. v3 adds an explicit claim of being first to combine exactness, efficiency, and compatibility with future-dependent pretokenization. Its contribution list qualifies distribution preservation by invalid-token probability mass, while the abstract drops v1's unqualified preservation wording.

C2.justification: v1 largely treats invalid-token mass as negligible. v3 distinguishes local from global validity and acknowledges contrary findings in Appendix D. It also explains beam failures, qualifies the cross-model efficiency comparison, and interprets byte-sampling slowdown relative to bytes per token. These substantially expand the discussion of assumptions and practical limitations.

D1.justification: v3 documents special-token mappings, digit-group handling, ignore_merges, normalization, added-token automata, and tested tokenizer families. It also discloses the independent 25-million-character samples underlying conversion factors. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although v3 omits the explicit ByteSampler repository link provided in v1.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises positioning around tokenizer compatibility and the assumptions of competing exact methods. It incorporates canonical-generation work by Chatzi and Vieira, conflicting evidence about invalid segmentations from Geh and Vieira, and self-distillation research. This changes the scientific comparison with prior work beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten and reorganized. v3 presents covering-tree definitions and applications before their properties and streaming implementation, replaces the introductory example, and restructures the appendices. Existing tree examples move from Appendix D to G, and advanced decoding moves from E to F.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, rearranges existing diagrams, adds a next-byte probability illustration, and redesigns the comparison table. The BPE walkthrough table is replaced by pseudocode, seven experimental tables are added, and the retained example trees are relocated. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for central claims: v1's token-count efficiency evidence is supplemented with measured runtimes and a same-model overhead comparison, while invalid-token assumptions and boundary-sensitive code completion receive direct tests. The revised distribution analysis and uncertainty reporting improve interpretability. Repeated baseline labels in Table 14, inconsistent complexity descriptions, and omission of the code link weaken parts of the revision, but the overall evidential gains are substantial.
